opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here.

Scene understanding has improved enormously in the last few years. Vision-language models and the large pretrained vision systems can look at a cluttered kitchen counter and tell you, with surprising accuracy, that there's a mug, a sponge, and a half-open bag of chips, and roughly where each one is. That's a real step forward. Fifteen years ago, segmenting objects in a messy scene was a research problem in itself, and now it's something you can more or less download.

But I want to be careful, because there's a tendency to assume that if a robot can *see* and *describe* a scene, it can *act* in it. Those are very different things. Knowing there's a mug on the table doesn't tell you how to grasp it, how much force to apply, what happens when your fingers make contact, or how the mug will slide or tip if you nudge it slightly off-center. Manipulation is fundamentally about physics: friction, contact, mass distribution. Tiny errors of a millimeter or two can be the difference between success and failure. And much of that is invisible to a camera. You can't see the coefficient of friction or the center of mass.

This is a version of Moravec's paradox. Things that seem hard for humans, like playing chess or passing exams, turned out to be relatively easy for computers, while things a toddler does effortlessly, like picking up an unfamiliar object, remain extremely hard for robots.

So I see the scene-interpretation models as a very valuable layer, because they give the robot semantic context: what things are, what the task is, what "clean up the table" might mean. That's helpful for high-level planning. But the low-level problem of reliable grasping and dexterous manipulation still needs something more. In our lab, with projects like Dex-Net, we've combined learning with physics and analytic models of grasping, and I think that hybrid approach, good old-fashioned engineering together with learning, is going to matter for a while.

There's also the data question. Language models were trained on essentially the whole internet, an enormous amount of text. There's no equivalent internet of robot manipulation data. People are trying to close that gap with simulation, teleoperation, and video of humans, and there's real progress there. But I think the gap is much bigger than many people appreciate, and we should be realistic about the timelines. I'm optimistic, but I'd say the progress will be steady and incremental rather than a sudden leap to robots that can do everything in your home.

r001.rationale: It says scene models identify objects and interpret what a task such as “clean up the table” might mean, but does not clearly say they identify which scene parts are relevant to the user’s requested task.

r002.rationale: It describes combining learning with physics and analytic grasping models, but does not identify combining deep learning, sensors, and hardware as a route to better manipulation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most exciting developments we've seen, and I say that as someone who's been in robotics for a long time and has learned to be skeptical of hype. For decades, perception was the bottleneck. If you wanted a robot to pick something up, you had to tell it exactly what the object was, where it was, often with fiducial markers or carefully controlled lighting. The robot essentially saw nothing. It was operating in a world we'd pre-digested for it.

What's changed is that these vision-language models and foundation models for perception can look at a cluttered scene, a kitchen counter or a warehouse bin, and give you a semantically meaningful description. This is a mug, it's upside down, it's behind the cereal box, the handle is facing away. That kind of understanding was science fiction ten years ago. And it matters enormously for manipulation because so much of grasping is really about knowing what you're dealing with. If you know it's a wine glass, you grasp it differently than if it's a hammer.

But I want to be careful here, because I think there's a tendency to assume that once perception is solved, manipulation follows automatically. It doesn't. There's something I've called Moravec's paradox that still haunts us. The things that are hard for humans, like playing chess or passing the bar exam, turn out to be relatively easy for machines, and the things a two-year-old does effortlessly, like picking up a toy from a pile, remain remarkably difficult. Scene interpretation gets you to the point of knowing what to do. It doesn't tell you how to do it. The physics of contact, friction, deformable objects, uncertainty in your own actuators, all of that is still there once you've identified the object.

So I'd describe these models as giving us a tremendously better front end. In our own work on grasping, we used to spend enormous effort just on segmentation, figuring out where one object ends and another begins. Now that's largely handled, and we can focus on the hard part, which is the actual interaction with the physical world. I'd also add that the language component is underappreciated. Being able to say to a robot, "hand me the thing I'd use to open this bottle," and have it reason about that, that's a genuine qualitative shift in how we can interface with these systems.

Where I remain cautious is on the data side. These perception models were trained on billions of images from the internet. There is no equivalent internet of manipulation data. There's no corpus of a billion grasps with force feedback. So the perception side is racing ahead, and the control side is still, in many ways, in the era of scarce data. Closing that gap is, I think, the central challenge for the next decade.

r001.rationale: The response says models can describe objects and reason about a language request, but it does not clearly state that they identify which scene parts are relevant to that task.

r002.rationale: It discusses perception models and physical-control challenges, but does not identify combining deep learning, sensors, and hardware as a route to better manipulation.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re a very exciting part of the story. To manipulate an object, a robot needs to understand something about what it’s looking at: where the object is, how it’s oriented, and which parts might be accessible. Models that interpret scenes can help enormously with that, and with connecting a human request to the right object.

But there’s a gap between understanding an image and knowing how to act. If you’re picking up a glass, you need to know where to put your fingers, how much force to apply, and whether it’s starting to slip. Some of those properties aren’t visible. You discover them through contact.

So I see these models as providing a much better starting point for manipulation. The robot still needs to act, get feedback, and adjust. The exciting possibility is combining that richer visual understanding with control that can handle uncertainty, rather than requiring the robot to understand everything perfectly before it moves.

r001.rationale: It says scene interpretation can connect a human request to the right object, communicating selection of the scene element relevant to the task.

r002.rationale: It describes combining visual understanding with control, but does not identify advances in deep learning, sensors, and hardware as the route to better manipulation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re a very promising ingredient. A robot has to make sense of what it’s looking at before it can decide where to grasp, and these models can give it a much richer interpretation of a scene. You can imagine saying, “Pick up the mug,” and having the system identify which object you mean, even in an unfamiliar environment.

But there’s a gap between understanding an image and successfully manipulating what’s in it. Where exactly should the fingers go? Is the object slippery? What happens when you make contact? Some of that information simply isn’t available in the image. The robot needs to act, get feedback, and adjust.

So I’m excited about combining these models with methods for planning and control that explicitly account for uncertainty. Better scene interpretation can help enormously, but we still have to close that loop between perception and physical action.

r001.rationale: It says the system can identify which object is meant when asked to “Pick up the mug,” including in an unfamiliar environment.
